learn: The three components of every ML algorithm and the practical ML loop
Attribute types (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) and data types
Aggregation, cleansing, imputation; IQR and 3-sigma outlier rules with worked examples
Min-max, z-score and decimal scaling with worked examples
Feature extraction, selection, construction, discretisation and encoding
intro.why: Model quality is bounded by data quality. Most real-project time goes into these steps, and most silent failures (leakage, distorted scales, invented orders) originate here.
prereq: Basic Python/pandas helps for the code

symbols: minimum and maximum of attribute $A$ (training data)
fence multiplier (1.5 for IQR, 3 for sigma)

sections.title: Components of an ML algorithm and ML in practice
sections.plain: Representation, optimisation, evaluation, inside a loop.
sections.body:
There are tens of thousands of ML algorithms, with hundreds new each year, but every one has three components: data representation, parameter optimisation, and model evaluation and selection.

ML in practice is a loop: understand the domain, prior knowledge and goals → data integration, selection, cleaning, preprocessing → learn optimal model parameters → interpret results → consolidate and deploy discovered knowledge → repeat.

sections.title: Data, objects and attribute types
sections.plain: Rows are objects; columns are attributes of a type.
sections.body:
Data is a collection of data objects and their attributes. An attribute (variable, field, characteristic, dimension, feature) is a property of an object; a collection of attributes describes an object (record, point, case, sample, entity, instance). Example table: Tid, Refund, Marital status, Taxable income, Cheat.

TypeMeaningful operationsExamples
Nominal$=,\ne$ID numbers, zip codes
Ordinal$<,>$Rankings (taste 1–10), grades, height {tall, medium, short}
Interval$+,-$Calendar dates, °C, °F
Ratio$\times,\div$Kelvin, length, counts, elapsed time

Each type supports all operations of the types above it. Discrete attributes take finitely or countably many values (zip codes, counts, words in documents), usually integers; binary attributes are a special case. Continuous attributes take real values (temperature, height, weight), measured with finite precision and stored as floating point.

sections.title: Characteristics of data and data types
sections.plain: Dimensionality, sparsity, resolution, size; many data shapes.
sections.body:
Characteristics: dimensionality (high-dimensional data brings challenges), sparsity (only presence counts), resolution (patterns depend on scale), size (the type of analysis may depend on it).

Data typeExample
Relational / objectCustomers with service rating (discrete numeric), is-priority (binary), card type (ordinal), credit score (continuous), multiple-account holder (binary)
TransactionalMarket baskets: items bought per transaction
DocumentTerm counts per document (trend, data, story, mining, cloth)
Web & social networkPeople as nodes with work field, purpose, domain, connections
SpatialCall records with tower cell ID, latitude, longitude
Time seriesProfit %, attrition rate, credit score by quarter
SequenceDNA base sequences

Case study 1: a bank segments customers by account information for targeted marketing, then targets high-income customers holding premium cards. Attributes: name, gender (nominal), service rating (ordinal/discrete), is-priority (binary), card type (ordinal), credit score (continuous), multiple accounts (binary), income level (ordinal), region (nominal).

sections.title: Data quality: dimensions, noise and outliers
sections.plain: Quality has six dimensions; noise and outliers are different things.
sections.body:
Quality dimensions: correct, complete, consistent, trustworthy, interpretable, usable on demand. Questions: what kinds of problems, how to detect them, what to do. Examples: noise and outliers, wrong data, fake data, missing values, duplicate data.

Noise: for objects, an extraneous object; for attributes, modification of original values (voice distortion on a poor line, television "snow"). Two sine waves plus random noise: the magnitude and shape of the original signal are distorted.

Outliers: objects with characteristics considerably different from most others. Case 1: noise that interferes with analysis. Case 2: the goal of the analysis (credit-card fraud, intrusion detection).

sections.title: Preprocessing overview
sections.body:
Preprocessing involves data engineering (raw data → prepared data) and feature engineering (prepared data → engineered features expected by the model) before ML.

Case study: a work-integrated M.Tech programme with partner IT companies wants to estimate how many students will be eligible for the dissertation semester so that billing documentation can be prepared. Attributes include name, gender, age, date of birth, organisation, job title, entrance and eligibility scores, previous degree, batch, section and course grades. Challenge 1: insufficient training data; idea: trade-off between algorithm sophistication and data readiness.

Steps: data aggregation, data cleansing, instance selection and partitioning, feature tuning.

sections.title: Data aggregation
sections.body:
Example: transactions recording daily product sales in stores across cities (Minneapolis, Chicago, Paris). Aggregate to reduce data, change scale (city, region) and stabilise variation (aggregated values vary less).

Group-by: split by key "color" (white: 12, 8; red: 20, 14; black: 6, 10), apply mean, combine → white 10, red 17, black 8.

sections.title: Data cleansing and imputing missing values
sections.plain: Correct or remove bad records; impute gaps deliberately.
sections.body:
Remove or correct corrupted or invalid records:

  • Noisy: errors or outliers, e.g. Salary = −10.
  • Inconsistent: Age = 42 with birthday 03/07/2010; ratings changed from 1,2,3 to A,B,C; discrepancies between duplicates.
  • Intentional: disguised missing data (1 January as everyone's birthday).
  • Records missing a large number of columns; duplicate data.

Table example: a 10,000K income ("a mistake or a millionaire?"), NULL marital status and NULL label (missing values), and two inconsistent duplicate rows (same person, different marital status).

Imputation options: insert missing records, replace with 0, replace with last known value, replace with the mean, interpolate (e.g. splines). On the monthly series the mean (284.5) is far from neighbouring values (~130), which shows why the mean is a poor choice for trending series.

sections.title: Univariate outliers: IQR and 3-sigma
sections.plain: Fences at Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR, or μ ± 3σ.
sections.body:
IQR rule: $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$; lower bound $Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$, upper bound $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$. Example: $Q_1=10,\ Q_3=20\Rightarrow\text{IQR}=10$, bounds $-5$ and $35$.

Exercisewith quartile positions $\frac14(n+1)$ and $\frac34(n+1)$. Sorted data used: 10, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 17, 22 ($n=12$).

  1. Median $Q_2=(12+13)/2=12.5$.
  2. $Q_1$ at position 3.25 → 11.
  3. $Q_3$ at position 9.75 → $14+0.75(15-14)=14.75$; a commonly quoted version uses 14.5.
  4. With the values: IQR = 3.5, fences 5.75 and 19.75 → outlier 22.

The exercise's raw data lists "2" but the sorted list treats it as "12". If 2 is genuine, it is also an outlier (below 5.75). Different quartile conventions (14.5 vs 14.75) change the fence slightly but not the conclusion.

3-sigma rule: lower $\mu-3\sigma$, upper $\mu+3\sigma$. Example: $\mu=50,\sigma=5$ → fences 35 and 65. For a normal distribution about 99.7% of values lie within $\pm3\sigma$ (a commonly quoted version says 99%). The figure also shows Tukey's IQR fences at $\pm2.698\sigma$ for normal data.

sections.title: Instance selection, partitioning and sampling
sections.body:
Partition into training, validation and test sets. Challenge 2: non-representative training data. Small samples cause sampling noise (increase sample size); flawed sampling causes bias even with large samples. A sample works almost as well as the full data if it is representative, i.e. has approximately the same properties of interest (a commonly quoted version shows an image at 8000, 2000 and 500 points).

Random split pitfall: Iris (50/50/50) split 2/3–1/3 at random gave training 38 Setosa, 28 Versicolor, 34 Virginica and test 12, 22, 16. Class proportions shifted noticeably; stratified sampling keeps them at 1/3 each.

Sampling types: simple random, stratified, clustered. Imbalanced training set: modify the training distribution so the rare class is well represented: under-sample the majority class or over-sample the rare class. Supplementary SMOTE synthesises minority points by interpolating between neighbours; class weights are an alternative that leaves data unchanged. Never rebalance the test set.

sections.title: Feature scaling: normalisation vs standardisation
sections.plain: Map to a range, or to standard units.
sections.body:
Min-max normalisation to $[\text{new}_{\min},\text{new}_{\max}]$:

$$v'=\frac{v-\min_A}{\max_A-\min_A}(\text{new}_{\max}-\text{new}_{\min})+\text{new}_{\min}$$

Example: income range \$12,000–\$98,000 to [0, 1]: $\frac{73{,}600-12{,}000}{98{,}000-12{,}000}=0.716$.

Z-score standardisation: $v'=\dfrac{v-\mu_A}{\sigma_A}$. Example: $\mu=54{,}000,\ \sigma=16{,}000$: $\frac{73{,}600-54{,}000}{16{,}000}=1.225$.

Decimal scaling: $v'=v/10^j$ with $j$ the smallest integer such that $\max|v'|<1$.

When to use which: normalisation when bounds are approximately known, data roughly uniform (age, not skewed income), and the algorithm makes no distributional assumption (k-NN, neural nets); ranges [0,1] or [−1,1]. Standardisation when the algorithm assumes Gaussian-like data, not bounded, less affected by outliers. Scaling target values is generally not required. Fit scalers on training data only and use them to transform training and test sets.

sections.title: Feature engineering: extraction, selection, construction
sections.body:
Feature engineering produces a good feature set and removes irrelevant ones.

  • Extraction: reduce the number of features by creating lower-dimensional ones. As dimensionality increases, data becomes sparse in the space it occupies (curse of dimensionality). Solution: dimensionality reduction, e.g. PCA.
  • Selection: choose a subset of input features: handle redundant features, remove irrelevant ones, drop features missing many values. In the student case: drop name, gender, age, date of birth, organisation, job title, nature of job, scores, batch, section; keep previous degree and course grades. Code: df.drop(['COL1','COL2'], axis=1).
  • Construction: polynomial expansion (univariate functions), feature crossing (interactions), business-logic features. Example: Customer_Lifetime = Last_Purchase_Date − First_Purchase_Date.

sections.title: Transformations: discretisation, binning and encoding
sections.plain: Bins for numbers, codes for categories.
sections.body:
Transform: e.g. replace semester totals with semester GPA or completion flags.

Discretisation: convert a continuous attribute into interval labels (0–10, 11–20) or conceptual labels (youth, adult, senior). Why: naïve Bayes, decision trees, random forests and minimum-distance/k-NN classifiers can prefer discrete features; also called binning or bucketing; handles outliers; improves value spread.

Binning: equal-width: $N$ intervals of width $W=(B-A)/N$, where $A$ and $B$ are the lowest and highest values; straightforward, but outliers may dominate and skewed data is handled poorly. Equal-depth (frequency): $N$ intervals each with about the same number of samples; good data scaling.

Encoding categorical features: one-hot / dummy maps a category to binary columns (Fuel ∈ {Gas, Diesel} → Gas, Diesel columns). Label encoding maps categories to integers (Gas → 1, Diesel → 2). The last row "gas" (lowercase) becomes a third code (3): uncleaned data creates spurious categories. Supplementary Label encoding implies an order, which suits ordinal data and tree models but misleads linear and distance-based models on nominal data. With one-hot and an intercept, drop one column to avoid perfect multicollinearity (the dummy-variable trap).

sections.title: Pipelines, leakage and complexity
sections.plain: Put every fitted transform inside the cross-validated pipeline.
sections.body:
Every step that learns from data (imputer means, scaler statistics, encoder categories, PCA components, feature selection) must be fitted on training folds only. Wrap them in a pipeline so cross-validation refits them per fold.

PIPELINE
  numeric:  impute(median) → scale(standard)
  nominal:  impute(most frequent) → one-hot(handle_unknown=ignore)
  ordinal:  map to ordered integers
  model:    estimator
fit(train) ; evaluate(test)        # never fit on test

Complexity: scaling, imputation and one-hot encoding are $O(nd)$; quartiles need sorting, $O(n\log n)$ per feature; PCA is $O(nd^2+d^3)$. One-hot can explode memory for high-cardinality columns; use hashing or target encoding (with care for leakage).

sections.title: Common technical misconceptions
sections.body:
• "Standardisation makes data normal." It only shifts and rescales; the shape stays the same.
  • "Min-max is robust." A single extreme value compresses everything else into a tiny range.
  • "3-sigma works for any distribution." It assumes approximate normality; for skewed data use IQR or robust z-scores (median and MAD).
  • "Mean imputation is harmless." It shrinks variance and weakens correlations; add a missing-indicator column when missingness is informative.
  • "Over-sampling before the split is fine." Duplicated minority points then leak into the test set.
  • "Trees need scaling." Tree splits are invariant to monotone transformations; distance- and gradient-based models need it.

code.title: Outliers with IQR and 3-sigma exercise
code.explain: Applies the quartile convention and NumPy's default to the exercise data, with and without the suspicious '2'.
mistakes: Assuming every library uses the same percentile method.
Removing outliers before checking whether they are the signal.
code.notes: pandas' quantile and NumPy's percentile default to linear interpolation; the (n+1) convention matches many textbooks.
code.code:
import numpy as np

def quartiles_n_plus_1(x):
    """Quartiles at positions (n+1)/4 and 3(n+1)/4 of the sorted data (convention)."""
    s = np.sort(x); n = len(s)
    def at(pos):                      # 1-based position with linear interpolation
        lo = int(np.floor(pos)); frac = pos - lo
        return s[lo - 1] + frac * (s[lo] - s[lo - 1]) if lo < n else s[-1]
    return at((n + 1) / 4), at(3 * (n + 1) / 4)

def iqr_outliers(x, k=1.5, method="n+1"):
    q1, q3 = quartiles_n_plus_1(x) if method == "n+1" else np.percentile(x, [25, 75])
    lo, hi = q1 - k * (q3 - q1), q3 + k * (q3 - q1)
    return [round(float(v), 2) for v in (q1, q3, lo, hi)], [v for v in x if v < lo or v > hi]

as_sorted_on_slide = [10, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 17, 22]
as_listed_on_slide = [10, 2, 11, 15, 11, 14, 13, 17, 12, 22, 14, 11]
for name, d in [("sorted list", as_sorted_on_slide), ("raw list", as_listed_on_slide)]:
    print(name, "| (n+1) rule Q1, Q3, fences, outliers:", iqr_outliers(d))
    print(name, "| numpy default            :", iqr_outliers(d, method="numpy"))

x = np.array(as_sorted_on_slide, float)
print("3-sigma fences:", round(float(x.mean() - 3 * x.std()), 2), round(float(x.mean() + 3 * x.std()), 2))

raw list | (n+1) rule Q1, Q3, fences, outliers: ([11.0, 14.75, 5.38, 20.38], [2, 22])

code.title: Scaling with the worked numbers, fitted on training data only
code.explain: Reproduces 0.716 (min-max) and 1.225 (z-score), then shows the correct fit/transform pattern.
mistakes: Calling fit_transform on the test set.
code.notes: Keep fitted scalers with the model; production data must use the same statistics.
code.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler

# Reference numbers: income range 12,000-98,000; mean 54,000, sd 16,000; value 73,600
print("min-max :", round((73_600 - 12_000) / (98_000 - 12_000), 3))
print("z-score :", round((73_600 - 54_000) / 16_000, 3))
print("decimal :", 73_600 / 10**5)          # j = 5 is the smallest with |v'| < 1

# Correct pattern: learn statistics on training data only
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = rng.lognormal(mean=10.8, sigma=0.4, size=(1000, 1))
train, test = income[:800], income[800:]
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(train)               # fit on train
z_train, z_test = scaler.transform(train), scaler.transform(test)
print("train mean/sd after scaling:", z_train.mean().round(3), z_train.std().round(3))
print("test  mean/sd after scaling:", z_test.mean().round(3), z_test.std().round(3), "(not exactly 0/1: expected)")
mm = MinMaxScaler().fit(train)
print("test values outside [0,1] after min-max:", int(((mm.transform(test) < 0) | (mm.transform(test) > 1)).sum()))

code.title: Stratified vs random split, and a preprocessing pipeline
code.explain: Shows class proportions after random and stratified splits of Iris, and a ColumnTransformer that imputes, scales and one-hot encodes mixed data.
mistakes: Encoding categories with LabelEncoder for a linear model.
code.notes: handle_unknown='ignore' keeps the pipeline working when unseen categories appear in production.
code.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
for strat in (None, y):
    _, _, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=1/3, random_state=1, stratify=strat)
    print("stratified" if strat is not None else "random    ", "train counts", np.bincount(y_tr), "test counts", np.bincount(y_te))

df = pd.DataFrame({"income": [125, 100, 70, np.nan, 95], "fuel": ["Gas", "Diesel", "gas", "Gas", None]})
df["fuel"] = df["fuel"].str.capitalize()                         # clean before encoding
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), ["income"]),
    ("cat", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")), ["fuel"])])
out = prep.fit_transform(df)
print(prep.get_feature_names_out().tolist())
print(np.round(out, 2))
